title: The wartime refuge of Norway’s royals
gist: A memorial note on Norway's King Harald V (reign 1991–2026, died 28 August) recounting the 1940 German invasion of Norway, the royal family's exile to Britain guarded by the Yorkshire Green Howards, and the resulting tradition of Norwegian monarchs as the regiment's Colonels-in-Chief. It highlights the strategic logic of Operation Weserübung and the durability of royal popularity.

themes.theme: Strategic logic of the 1940 invasion of Norway

insights.claim: Germany invaded Norway on 9 April 1940 to secure ice-free harbours for controlling the North Atlantic, protect the trade routes carrying Swedish iron ore, and pre-empt an Anglo-French move with the same aims.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Scandinavian ports and northern raw-material routes remain strategic prizes; relevant to today's High North and Baltic security premium.
insights.quote: aiming to secure ice-free harbours from which to control the North Atlantic, secure the trade routes used to transport iron ore from Sweden

insights.claim: Both German and Allied naval forces ignored Norwegian neutrality and arrived off the Scandinavian coast simultaneously in April 1940, as the Allies were planning to mine Norwegian waters, leading to clashes costly for the Kriegsmarine.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Neutral states on strategic sea lanes face pre-emption from both sides once great-power war begins.

insights.claim: Relying on neutrality after staying out of the First World War, Norway was ill-prepared for invasion, though it sank the heavy cruiser Blücher in Oslofjord on the first day; Norwegian casualties in Operation Weserübung were barely 1,000, British nearly 2,000, French and Poles around 500, and German over 5,000.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Complacency born of past neutrality left a strategically placed state exposed, a lesson echoed in Nordic rearmament debates.
insights.quote: Norway had stayed out of the First World War, and most assumed it would ride out the Second as well.
insights.locator: To most, the invasion had come

insights.claim: Resistance sprang up across Norway almost immediately after the 1940 invasion, including underground newspapers, smuggling people to Sweden and the UK, and sabotage, supported by the 'Shetland Bus' fishing vessels running weapons and agents from Scotland.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for societal resistance planning that informs current Nordic total-defence concepts.

insights.claim: After the war around 50,000 Norwegians who had collaborated with the Nazis under Vidkun Quisling's Nasjonal Samling were found guilty of treason, of whom 25 were shot.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Illustrates the scale of collaboration even in a society with strong resistance.

themes.theme: Anglo-Norwegian royal-military bond and monarchy's legitimacy

insights.claim: Because the Yorkshire Green Howards guarded Norway's exiled royal family in 1940, every Norwegian monarch since 1942 has been Colonel-in-Chief of the regiment, and an honour guard of its successor, the Royal Yorkshire Regiment, attended Harald V's state funeral on 9 September.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Symbolic military ties underpin the durability of UK-Norway security cooperation.

insights.claim: King Harald V's approval ratings hovered in the 70s for most of his 1991–2026 reign; his coffin was visited by 46,000 people while lying in state and nearly 100 countries were represented at his funeral.
insights.speaker: Peter Caddick-Adams
insights.so_what: Signals stable institutional legitimacy in Norway through the royal succession.
